We argue that this may represent a fundamental shift in how we produce, use, and evaluate research artifacts in the technical HCI community.

title: When to Use Subagents
abstract: When should a task be delegated to subagents? We answer this at the granularity of individual trajectories. Modeling a trajectory as a dependency graph, we identify bridge edges, whose removal separates the trajectory into independent components, and show that the agent orchestration pattern should match this bridge-edge structure. Our experiments on long-horizon benchmarks indicate that subagents tend to benefit sparse bridge-edge structures, whereas tightly coupled trajectories are often better handled by a single agent. We instantiate this principle as SAIGE, a lightweight mechanism that spawns subagents only at predicted bridge edges and resolves their connections lazily, achieving a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance where the structure admits decomposition. We further observe that scaling the agent pool or recursion depth does not reliably help, in line with the view that orchestration should follow the bridge-edge pattern.

title: The Software Engineering Factory: Engineering Accountability and Control in the Age of Abundant Code
abstract: AI agents can now plan, write, test, review, and revise code at a volume no human organization can inspect line by line. Final code review therefore cannot remain the primary organizational control for owning code changes. The Software Engineering (SE) Factory moves control into the process that produces the code. The Factory protocols define how work moves, what evidence must exist before it can proceed, and who owns the result. A deterministic protocol engine, implemented in conventional code rather than prompts, enforces those protocols by controlling stage transitions, requiring evidence, and invoking gates and human escalation, where needed, before work can advance. The SE Factory preserves human authority over consequential decisions and makes accountable acceptance possible without requiring humans to supervise every agent action. The SE Factory is not a dark factory. Humans remain in control by defining the scope and granularity of delegation, the boundaries and escalation conditions, and the consequential decisions that require accountable human judgment. We draw on our experience building three distinct SE Factory implementations, all of which have undergone multiple iterations and two of which are publicly available as open-source systems, into ten principles for conceiving, building, and operating SE Factories at scale, grounded in the organizational and technical realities of our implementations. We do not claim that these principles are exhaustive or constitute the only viable foundation for an SE Factory. Rather, we offer them as a conceptual scaffold and shared vocabulary for reasoning about SE Factories, evaluating their designs, and guiding their evolution. Our goal is to catalyze a community-wide dialogue that moves software engineering beyond controls designed for human-scale code production toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

title: Shared Organizational Memory for Enterprise Coding Agents: System Design and Deployment Snapshot
abstract: Enterprise coding agents rely on tools and retrieval, yet enterprise knowledge often remains outside public training data and formal documentation: internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, and tacit workflows. Existing knowledge interfaces expose stored resources but still depend on agents recognizing and explicitly recording lessons worth reusing, disconnecting capture from the coding workflow and leaving development experience repeatedly rediscovered. We report an ongoing production deployment of a shared organizational memory system that makes capture a platform-level part of coding work: it collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates it into reusable question-answer memories, gates obvious security and privacy risks, and retrieves memories for future agents. This short paper describes the deployed lifecycle and an operational snapshot. Effects on retrieval and coding tasks remain under evaluation.

title: The Tasteful Agent: Measuring and Improving Taste in Long-Horizon Tasks
abstract: LLM agents increasingly work on long-horizon tasks, and the decisions they make along the way, such as which hypothesis to test or which implementation to build on, determine the outcome of the whole run. Making these decisions well is becoming a key capability for both engineering and research agents. We refer to the ability to make good long-horizon decisions as the taste of an agent. While existing benchmarks measure the end-to-end success of agents on long-horizon tasks, none of them measures the taste of an agent. To address this problem, we build Taste-Bench, a benchmark of taste questions constructed automatically from trajectories that agents produced in engineering and research tasks. Each question presents a decision fork, a point in a trajectory where multiple directions are available and one of them leads to a better outcome, and the evaluated model chooses among these directions without seeing what happens after the fork. We mine these forks automatically from parallel attempts at the same task and from detours inside a single trajectory, without needing human annotation. We evaluate frontier models on Taste-Bench and find that the best model answers only 59.7% of the questions correctly. We further find that forks whose deciding evidence appears later in the trajectory are much harder for every model, and that a larger reasoning budget does not improve the accuracy. Finally, we show that taste can be trained. We distill the judgment of a teacher that has seen the outcome into a student model, and the student makes better decisions on unseen tasks and improves end-to-end success on held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks.

title: Problem Reductions at Scale: Agentic Integration of Computationally Hard Problems
abstract: Solving an NP-hard optimization problem often requires reformulating it for a specific solver -- quantum hardware, a commercial optimizer, or a domain heuristic. A tool for polynomial-time reductions between hard problems would let practitioners route any supported problem to any supported solver through a single interface. Building such a library at scale, however, has remained out of reach. We show that harness engineering, the practice of designing constraints, verification systems, and feedback loops that channel AI coding agents, can overcome this barrier. Our harness combines a no-code contribution route for domain experts, a multilayer verification stack ranging from type-level checks to agentic feature tests (AI agents role-playing as end users), and a fully automated implementation-review-integration pipeline. In about three months, we built a command-line tool backed by a library of 100+ problem types and 200+ reduction rules in over 170k lines of Rust. The result suggests that a well-engineered harness lets agents build well-tested software at a scale and pace beyond prior reduction-library efforts. Because the reduction graph composes transitively, a new solver registered for any single problem type instantly becomes available to every problem connected by a reduction path. The source code is available at https://github.com/CodingThrust/problem-reductions.

title: Agent 4: Teamwork and Collaboration for Vibe-Coding
abstract: As AI coding agents grow more capable, a natural path to scaling their throughput is to apply the same collaborative patterns—branching, parallel development, and merging—that human engineering teams have long relied on. However, multi-agent concurrency amplifies coordination challenges such as merge conflicts, duplicated work, and semantic inconsistencies, particularly on platforms like Replit where users describe intent in natural language rather than formal specifications. We present Agent 4’s teamwork architecture, which addresses these challenges through three layers: a planning agent decomposes user requests into a dynamic directed acyclic graph of tasks, using codebase exploration and an interview-driven workflow to minimize downstream conflicts. Isolated task agents execute each unit of work on a fully forked copy of the application state—filesystem, database, and configuration—enabled by Replit’s copy-on-write storage infrastructure, while lightweight intra-task subagents exploit finer-grained parallelism on a shared filesystem. A multi-layered validation pipeline comprising type checking, replayable regression tests derived from a REPL-based browser testing engine, and automated code review guards against logical drift before changes are merged back via an incremental rebasing strategy.

title: Claim Plane: Reliability Gains and the Limits of Selective Concurrency for Parallel Coding Agents: A 30-Pair, Three-Seed Confirmatory Study of Deterministic Pre-Write Admission
abstract: Parallel coding agents can produce locally valid changes that fail when combined. Claim Plane addresses this failure mode as deterministic pre-write admission over versioned change intents. This paper reports a confirmatory study on 30 frozen CooperBench feature pairs, balanced between 15 conflict and 15 clean labels, with three coder seeds, four coordination arms, and 360 completed executions. DeepSeek V4 Pro generated 60 feature-level planner declarations once; the declarations were frozen across all arms and coder seeds, while DeepSeek V4 Flash performed the coding work. Static Claim Plane raised pair pass from 23.3% under unconstrained parallel execution to 50.0%, a paired task-cluster difference of +26.7 percentage points (95% bootstrap CI 9.6 to 60.0), and raised integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%. On conflict-labeled pairs, pair pass rose from 6.7% to 60.0%. However, static admission serialized 96.7% of executions, including 93.3% of clean cases, and therefore recovered reliability largely by collapsing toward serial execution. Dynamic admission was more selective, serializing 66.7% of conflict cases and 13.3% of clean cases, but 46 of 90 executions failed closed on undeclared scope, reducing pair pass to 22.2%. Forty-five of those 46 blocks targeted files already present in the frozen declarations, indicating region undercoverage and insufficient amendment handling rather than wholly unknown files. The results support pre-write admission as a reliability mechanism, but they do not establish useful wall-clock parallel speedup: provider calls were physically sequential, and the conservative policy largely serialized the workload. The complete study artifacts, hashes, and clustered bootstrap analysis are publicly released for reproduction.

title: Pre-Compiled Codebase Knowledge Reduces LLM Query Cost by 71% While Improving Answer Quality
abstract: LLM coding agents answer developer questions through iterative source exploration: searching, reading files, and backtracking. This incurs high token costs and frequently fails on cross-cutting questions in large codebases. This paper presents a system that pre-compiles codebase knowledge into a structured wiki (API contracts, data flows, business rules) and a dependency graph (call chains, component relationships). At query time, a three-stage workflow (classify → select → answer) routes questions to the appropriate artifact and injects only relevant context. No source code access is required during answering. Evaluation on a 475-endpoint Go codebase across 21 queries shows 71% cost reduction (1.03 vs. 3.52 credits) while improving narrative comprehension F1 from 65% to 85%. The system achieves 100% bug localization accuracy on real GitHub issues without query-time source reads. Full replication materials: https://github.com/luvrama/gitea/tree/int-analysis-2/.wiki-eval/final-eval.

title: Conserved amount, negotiable placement. Prompting perturbs one architecture, an AI reviewer both
abstract: Tesler's conservation law holds that a problem carries an irreducible amount of complexity. Brooks separates that essential part from the accidental part a solution adds. If the essential part is fixed, architecture is placement rather than quantity, and the question is which levers move placement. An AI agent implements sixty accumulating change requests on one REST endpoint under two architectures, a mutative Spring controller and an additive OfficeFloor pipeline, under five conditions, ten runs per cell, model fixed. Four are external controls, from a bare change request to the disclosed structural cost function. The fifth is different in kind. A second agent reviews each change and reasons about cohesion itself. Amount is steady. Across all ten cells the finished complexity varies by 7% to 20% over four operationalisations, and the complexity the sixty rules added by 21% to 29% within an architecture. Placement is not. Under the four external controls the plasticity ratio between the architectures is near 1 on six amount metrics (five of six intervals contain 1) against 2.7 to 10.0 on eleven placement metrics (ten of eleven above 1). The mutative architecture moves, the additive one does not, and the disclosed formula brings it to the additive arm's untouched placement. The AI reviewer is the one lever that moves the additive arm, on one family only. It consolidates the pipeline, raising change- and mass-concentration on every such metric, interval excluding zero, while leaving coupling, file count and per-node complexity untouched. The price is reported in full. Strict correctness fell in most comparisons though each rule was implemented correctly in over 99% of checkpoints, and all three outcome measures favour the concentrated codebase. The contribution is a measurable property of an architecture and its lever, not a verdict on either.

title: EpiPlayBench: Executable Contract Testing for LLM-Generated Game Logic Grounded in SBML Models
LemonHarness Technical Report
abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents are applied to longer tasks, they increasingly modify workspace state across multiple rounds of iteration. However, agents typically observe only tool outputs and log fragments, while the actual state changes occur in the file system. Without explicit workspace boundaries, state-changing operations such as file writes and temporary artifact generation may scatter changes across paths. Over time, these weakly constrained changes accumulate, making states such as modified files difficult to track. This paper presents LemonHarness, an integrated execution framework for long-horizon agents. LemonHarness establishes an explicit execution boundary by constraining state-changing operations within a clearly defined workspace and bringing model invocation, tool execution, and rule knowledge within a single controlled boundary. State-changing operations, including file writes, dependency installation, and temporary artifact creation, are executed through structured tool interfaces, with execution feedback recorded as observations available to subsequent model decisions. The system also introduces a reusable rule knowledge base, which turns recurring execution rules and acceptance criteria into runtime knowledge. LemonHarness further adds a time-aware execution mechanism that exposes elapsed and remaining budget to the model, so it can rebalance exploration, implementation, and validation effort as time pressure shifts and avoid timeouts from long waits or excessive verification. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, LemonHarness_GPT-5.3-CodeX reached 84.49% accuracy over 445 trials; pairing the same framework with the stronger GPT-5.5 backbone raised the average accuracy to 86.52% across five jobs. The results suggest that a unified runtime boundary, callable rule knowledge, and time-aware execution can improve the stability of long-horizon agent execution.

title: Persistent Context Graphs for Efficient Memory Compaction in LLM Agents
abstract: As LLM capabilities advance, agents are tackling increasingly complex tasks over longer horizons. Their growing interaction histories make memory compaction essential for staying within context windows and reducing prefill cost. Existing methods summarize the history or compress its KV cache, often adding model computation to preserve information for future requests. A new user request can change which history matters, but reassessing that history with the model requires re-encoding it if the KV cache has expired. Past attention provides signals of historical importance and dependencies between messages, while relevance to the current task must be assessed using the new user request. We introduce ReCAP, a memory compaction method that stores attention-derived importance scores and dependency links in a lightweight, persistent context graph. For each new request, ReCAP combines stored importance with relevance cues from the request and follows dependency links to select messages and their supporting context, without additional model calls for selection. Compared with Codex's default summarization-based compaction, ReCAP reduces estimated latency for compaction and cold restoration by approximately 95% on both Qwen3-Coder and gpt-oss. It also roughly halves the historical context per call on SWE-Together at comparable task quality and improves accuracy on the code tasks of Lost-in-Conversation over full history by 19.8 and 41.2 points.

title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
abstract: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.

title: Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering
abstract: Coding agents increase implementation capacity without automatically making project intent, system structure, or acceptance evidence explicit. As implementation becomes abundant relative to engineering judgment, the scarce work shifts toward choosing useful abstractions, producing evidence, and determining which obligations govern acceptance. Existing workflows address parts of this gap through larger prompts, repository retrieval, or perchange review, but still require agents and engineers to reconstruct consequential properties. As an alternative, we present Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering (MAGE). MAGE is a framework and a theory for building trustworthy autonomy from commodity intelligence. MAGE addresses a representation problem and an authority problem: it externalizes the smallest purposeful representation needed to answer an engineering question, then gives settled obligations proportionate authority through constraints, sensors, validators, and gates. It keeps uncertain intent open and turns recurring reconstruction and judgment into durable engineering structure that later work can inherit. We developed MAGE from a longitudinal case and refined it through six independently reported industrial accounts. Across these sources, MAGE explains how externalized knowledge, bounded action, independent evaluation, and retained human authority can compose into a governed engineering environment, and proposes tests of when that environment turns commodity intelligence into durable engineering progress.

title: When Code Gets Cheap, Evaluation Gets Scarce: An Experience Report on AI-Assisted Agile Software Engineering
abstract: Coding assistants are widely reported to speed up code production; most accounts stop there. We report the end-to-end construction and deployment of a compliance-critical, human-in-the-loop exam-grading system, built by a single developer who wrote no code by hand, protected by a gated process from stakeholder persona to audited behavior. The initial system was built in three working days and could grade a real cohort. We draw one claim from this experience: AI changes software engineering less by making programming faster than by changing what is scarce. Writing code becomes abundant. Reliable evaluation-knowing whether a result is correct and meets the actual need-remains necessary at every iteration and becomes the binding constraint. Engineering judgment remains a second scarcity. Several defects passed the test suite: they sat at the boundaries the tests had mocked, the browser and the language-model API, or appeared only in real use. Deployment exposed assumptions that local tests had missed. Moreover, an AI assistant acting across many steps bypassed process checkpoints until we made them enforceable gates. All of this was observed in a triple union: the developer was also the end user and domain expert, making expert judgment immediately available and evaluation as cheap as it can be. This favors the iteration gains, which may shrink where evaluation requires additional people or expertise, but makes the case a hard test for evaluation scarcity: evaluation still constrained progress. We draw five lessons: run a gated, traceable construction process; specify what is knowable and discover the rest against a running prototype; validate in the real environment; gate the assistant, not only the work; record decisions with their assumptions and the process state the assistant forgets. A second project showed similar patterns; an independent single-expert case corroborates the shift.

title: DTOC: Dynamic Tool Output Compression for Adaptive Context Management in AI Agents
Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.

title: AgentBaton: Efficient Model Collaboration in Agentic Tasks
abstract: Solving long-horizon agentic tasks requires language agents to interact with their environments over multiple steps, and reliable performance often comes from the expensive capable models available through cloud providers. Meanwhile, alternative efficient models with inferior performance but a much lower cost are emerging, including lower-tier cloud models and smaller open-weights models deployable on local hardware. This raises a natural question that remains less explored than traditional query-level routing: can capable and efficient models collaborate within a single long-horizon agentic task to substantially reduce cost while preserving task accuracy? In this paper, we systematically investigate key design choices for such collaboration through model handoffs, where one model takes over from another, focusing on handoff direction and context transfer. We find that efficient-to-capable handoffs generally underperform capable-only execution with limited or even no cost reduction, whereas capable-to-efficient handoffs at suitable stages of task progress largely preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing cost. These findings suggest that a one-time, simple, well-timed handoff strategy is good enough for cost-effective agent collaboration, motivating AgentBaton, a lightweight detector that learns when to hand off from recurring patterns in task progress. Across 11 model pairs and two representative benchmarks, AgentBaton reduces API costs by 65.9% on average while largely preserving task accuracy, with accuracy gains of up to 8.8 percentage points over capable-only execution. Experiments across various reasoning-effort settings further show that AgentBaton extends the empirical accuracy-cost Pareto frontier.

title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
abstract: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

title: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Before Post-Training: An End-to-End Approach
abstract: Agentic capabilities are increasingly important for modern LLMs, yet remain difficult to evaluate during pretraining. Existing approaches typically rely on static trajectory-derived tasks or likelihood-based proxies, which are lightweight but provide limited visibility into how base models behave in interactive environments. We introduce ASAP (Agent Scaffold Adaptation for Pretraining Evaluation), a lightweight framework for eliciting and evaluating agentic behavior from pretrained base models on end-to-end tasks. Rather than converting base models into chat-style agents, ASAP preserves the completion interface and adapts existing agent scaffolds through structured trajectory continuation, short reference prefixes, and minimal recovery mechanisms. Across software-engineering and deep-research benchmarks, ASAP yields discriminative end-to-end performance across base models and pretraining checkpoints. Beyond aggregate scores, ASAP exposes model-generated execution trajectories, enabling analysis of exploration, editing, testing, recovery, and task completion across training stages. These trajectories provide a behavioral view of how agent-relevant capabilities change during pretraining and how execution patterns differ after post-training. Our results suggest that end-to-end agent evaluation can complement conventional pretraining benchmarks by providing a practical diagnostic of interactive model behavior.

title: AI Coding Benchmarks Need Composition Cards
abstract: Why the same model scores 70 percent and 6 percent, and what every benchmark should ship

title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
abstract: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.

title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.60. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

title: When Does Context Compaction Pay in Long-Horizon Agents?
abstract: Compacting an agent's history shortens later requests but can change the work needed to finish its task. We ask when early compaction pays after counting that change: only when a fixed-trace savings budget exceeds the cost of the changed work. We measure both with matched-state continuations to termination on nine long Terminal-Bench tasks, complete runs in two agent runtimes, and replays on a dedicated GPU deployment. At a 64K threshold, gpt-6.1-sol's budget was USD 0.17 per state, yet synchronous compaction (Sync) cost USD 0.26 more with measured cache reads. Added requests, mostly reads, exhausted the budget; the excess persisted across prompt, task, and runtime controls. With GLM-5.3-Flash, compaction saved. Cache prices set the budget: for our nine-task mix of complete 64K Sol runs, Sync would cost less only above a cache-read price of 34% of the uncached price, against a listed 5%. At one common price vector, savings appeared only where much work remained. On a dedicated GLM deployment, replayed Sync sessions took 30% less mean time than sessions keeping the full history at light load (3% with the work fixed) and at least 29% less at heavy load. At 102 concurrent sessions without a host-memory cache tier, waiting sessions' evicted prefixes had to be computed again, and Sync's work with the history restored took more than twice as long. We release an offline calibrator mapping complete-task usage and deployment prices to policy costs, price crossovers, and selection headroom.

title: AI Agents and Prompt Engineering in Econometric Coding
abstract: We study how large language models write econometric code.On 40 tasks in Stata, R, and Python, we vary the prompt (with or without an example) and the degree of agency (from a chatbot that only writes the script to an agent that also runs and revises it).For Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.6 Luna, the agent raises task success from 79 to 97 percent.Agent runs cost 3.1 to 5.0 times as much as chatbot runs.The example and the software matter more under the chatbot than under the agent, which removes most failures but only some wrong estimates

title: SWE-Critix: Post-Training Generalist Verifiers for Assessing Coding-Agent Trajectories
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly deployed for end-to-end software engineering tasks, where a readily available oracle evaluator that defines the success criteria is often absent. This motivates verifications for coding agents that can reliably judge and explain their behavior. However, verification is non-trivial as coding agents are increasingly capable of solving long-horizon software engineering tasks. Their execution trajectories can be extremely long, containing hundreds of iterative interactions with code repositories and external tools. Existing verifiers either rely on general-purpose LLMs without specialized training or train dedicated critics that predominantly focus on producing scalar rewards, highlighting the relatively limited exploration of training-based generalist verification. We introduce SWE-Critix, a post-training pipeline for training generalist verifiers of coding-agent trajectories. Given a task and its execution trajectory, the learned verifier predicts the completion label and generates a natural-language analysis that explains its judgment. Our pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) and trains a series of 30B models on trajectories from CodeForge-Preview. On a held-out test set, SWE-Critix improves classification accuracy from 57% for the base Qwen3-30B-A3B reasoning model to 66% after SFT and 78% after RL. We release our models, datasets, and training code to facilitate further research.

title: Assistance to Autonomy: A Systematic Literature Review of Agentic AI Across the Software Development Life Cycle
Using Process Mining to Generate AI Agents from Software Engineering Process Records
SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

title: The Impact of Modern AI on Software Development: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: As large language models, and agentic AI systems are increasingly being integrated into software engineering, an expanding amount of empirical evidence surrounding these technologies has emerged. This systematic literature review examines the impact of modern AI techniques and tools in software development lifecycle phases and related activities, covering studies published between 2023 and 2025 and resulting in a corpus of 62 primary studies, investigating the role of large language models, AI agents and agentic AI workflows across lifecycle phases. The synthesis is guided by three research questions that address the entire software development cycle, reported impacts on development practices, outcomes, and constraints. This review fills a gap in the synthesis of modern AI applications and their impacts. It concludes that modern AI in software engineering is progressively evolving from a generation tool into a reasoning and coordination infrastructure layer, with ongoing efforts targeting the mitigation of identified limitations and the advancement of trustworthy agentic AI capabilities for dependable software engineering practices.

title: Autonomous Evaluation Architectures: Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines, Browser-Grounded Testing: Programmatic Alignment via DSPy, and Adversarial Robustness in Production Orchestration Systems
When Clean Code Becomes Costly: Balancing Human Readability and AI Digestibility with the NUDEE Framework
abstract: Aim/Purpose: This study maps the structural tension between human-centric Clean Code conventions and the architectural demands of LLM-based coding agents. It proposes NUDEE, a management framework for governing codebases optimized for both human readability and AI digestibility. Background: Clean Code prescribes deep abstraction and module decomposition to reduce human memory load. By 2026, LLMs and autonomous agents actively participate in coding workflows, but their token-limited context windows are penalized by the same decomposition that helps human developers. Methodology: A PRISMA 2020-guided systematic literature review of three databases (Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library) used a three-pillar Boolean search strategy followed by four-stage screening. The resulting corpus of 89 records (1996–2026) was inductively coded into five thematic streams. Contribution: The paper presents a PRISMA-structured systematic literature review – to our knowledge, one of the first to systematically map the human-readability–AI digestibility tension in software engineering – documents the field’s organizational turn (44.9% of the literature addresses management frameworks) and introduces the NUDEE framework. Findings: The dominant stream, hybrid and agentic SE management frameworks (44.9%), confirms that the field has reframed the problem as organizational; synthesis across all streams reveals three structural pillars for AI-optimal codebases. Recommendations for Practitioners: Development teams should adopt the Software Coach and System Orchestrator roles, instrument the Context Efficiency Index in CI/CD pipelines to detect semantic debt early, and revise code review criteria to include digestibility alongside correctness. Recommendation for Researchers: Empirical validation of the CEI against real agent task-solve rates in production codebases is the field’s most pressing research need. Impact on Society: As AI agents increasingly execute code in critical systems, semantic debt in organizational codebases directly translates into reliability and safety risk. NUDEE provides a governance vocabulary that enables mid-size organizations, not only large technology firms, to manage human AI software knowledge assets responsibly. Future Research: CEI empirical validation with threshold calibration and longitudinal case studies testing whether teams adopting the dual-role model achieve higher agent reliability and shorter release cycles.

title: Design Problems, Decisions, and Evidence in Agentic Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
abstract: Agentic Software Engineering (ASE) systems depend on decisions about context, reasoning, coordination, tool use, execution, and verification. This systematic mapping study maps problems, design decisions, operationalizations, and evidence in peer-reviewed studies of LLM- or foundation-model-based agentic systems in Software Engineering from 1 January 2024 to 13 July 2026. ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Springer Nature Link were searched on 13 July 2026 using the same Boolean string. From 1069 records, 94 studies were included. A frozen, single-paper-isolated extraction protocol identified 1018 design decisions, followed by deterministic multi-label synthesis; no formal study-level risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Of these decisions, 633 were linked to 656 problems or objectives, and 913 (89.7%) had empirical or comparative evaluation records. Only 19.8% of evaluation records attributed evidence to an individual decision, whereas 52.3% assessed complete systems; multi-agent configurations represented 68.7% of problem-linked decisions. Heterogeneous metrics and system-level evaluation limit inference about effectiveness. The findings expose a gap between evaluation coverage and decision-level attribution and motivate ablations and human-centered evaluations. The review received no external funding and was not registered.

title: Integrating Large Language Models into PLC Programming: Algorithmic Execution and Validation Using MATLAB/Simulink
Generative AI for Software Engineering: A Review of Code Generation, Testing, Human–AI Collaboration, and Quality Assurance
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly reshaping software engineering (SE) across the development lifecycle. This review synthesises 113 peer-reviewed journal studies and organises the literature around five research questions and four application areas: code generation, testing and debugging, human–AI collaboration, and quality assurance. The reviewed studies show substantial progress in natural-language-to-code generation, context-aware programming, automated testing, fault localisation, program repair, and AI-assisted development. At the same time, persistent challenges remain in semantic correctness, non-deterministic outputs, software security, maintainability, verification, and evaluation consistency. Drawing these findings together, the paper presents a lifecycle mapping, a closed-loop AI-driven software engineering framework, and a four-dimension taxonomy to organise existing research and clarify connections across previously fragmented areas. Overall, generative AI is moving software engineering from a largely deterministic and human-centred workflow toward a more probabilistic and AI-enhanced engineering process. Further progress will depend on stronger verification, security, reliability, maintainability, and appropriately calibrated human oversight.

title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
abstract: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.

title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

title: AutoPCM: Automated Generation of Architectural Performance Models from Early Design Artifacts Using LLM Agents
Can AI Smell (Yet)? Anticipatory Judgment, Gap Closure, and the Lovelace Objection
AGENTIC TECHNICAL DEBT IN LLM-BASED CODE AGENTS: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW OF VERIFICATION, GOVERNANCE, AND LONG-TERM SUSTAINABILITY IN RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED IRAQI SOFTWARE ECOSYSTEMS
abstract: Background: The adoption rate of LLM-based code agents is exceeding the existing evidence on their implications for the long-term maintenance in the Iraqi software industry. Aim: This systematic literature review (SLR) provides an overview of the emerging concept of agentic technical debt (AgTD) and explores the nature of AgTD in the areas of verification, governance, and sustainability taking into account the constraints on resources characteristic of the Iraqi software ecosystem. Methods: Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and the Kitchenham-Charters SLR method, we conducted a search in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, arXiv, and Iraqi academic libraries (IASJ, Iraqi Journal for Computers and Informatics) from 1992 to 2026 and included 87 studies in the synthesis after screening. Results: The results reveal 31 AI technical debt types which can manifest themselves as agentic types, classified into seven root-cause categories. It becomes clear that verification and governance are under-researched areas as compared to code generation, and that agentic inputs need more corrective maintenance effort and generate more security flaws than human inputs. For resource-poor systems, three amplifiers—skill shortages, review capacity constraints, and weak infrastructure—aggravate the buildup of debt. Conclusion: We recommend a three-pronged AgTD management approach (Verify-Govern-Sustain) and research agenda for software engineering in Iraq. The review proves the AgTD construct and shows that sustainability in language model-assisted software development is a governance issue, not a code generation issue.

title: Toward Architecture-Aware Evaluation Metrics for LLM Agents
abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming central to software engineering tasks, yet evaluating them remains fragmented and largely model-centric. Existing studies overlook how architectural components—such as planners, memory, and tool routers—shape agent behavior, limiting diagnostic power. We propose a lightweight, architecture-informed approach that links agent components to their observable behaviors and to the metrics capable of evaluating them. Our method clarifies what to measure and why, and we illustrate its application through real world agents, enabling more targeted, transparent, and actionable evaluation of LLM-based agents.

title: Graphectory Viewer: A Tool for Process-Centric Analysis of Agentic Software Trajectories
abstract: We present Graphectory Viewer, a web-based tool for interactive, process-centric analysis of software-agent trajectories. Building on the Graphectory representation introduced in our previous work, Graphectory Viewer transforms heterogeneous raw trajectories into phase-aware graphs that connect low-level execution details with higher-level behavioral structures. The tool supports trajectories from multiple agent frameworks and provides interactive graph construction; node-level inspection of thoughts, actions, and observations; search and filtering over large trajectory collections; and Sankey-style summaries of problem-solving phase transitions. These capabilities enable researchers and practitioners to inspect individual executions, identify recurring behavioral patterns, compare successful and failed runs, and analyze large trajectory corpora beyond final task outcomes. To support reproducibility and further research, we release Graphectory Viewer as an open-source artifact together with documentation, precomputed graphs, and the large-scale trajectory corpus.

title: Why Human Guidance Matters in Collaborative Vibe Coding
abstract: Writing code has been one of the most transformative ways for human societies to translate abstract ideas into tangible technologies. Modern AI is changing this process by enabling experts and non-experts alike to generate code without actually writing it, instead using natural language instructions or "vibe coding". While increasingly popular, the impact of vibe coding on productivity and collaboration, and the role of humans in this process, remains unclear. Here, we introduce a controlled experimental framework for studying collaborative vibe coding and use it to compare human-led, AI-led, and hybrid groups. Across 20 experiments involving 737 human participants, we show that people provide uniquely effective high-level instructions for vibe coding, whereas AI-provided instructions often result in performance collapse. We further demonstrate that hybrid systems perform best when humans lead by providing instructions while evaluation is delegated to AI. Although AI systems can rapidly optimize performance for specific tasks, our work highlights the importance of human guidance in shaping future hybrid societies.

title: 1D-Bench: A Benchmark for Iterative UI Code Generation with Visual Feedback in Real-World
abstract: Design-to-code translates high-fidelity UI designs into executable front-end implementations, but progress remains hard to compare due to inconsistent datasets, toolchains, and evaluation protocols. We introduce 1D-Bench, a benchmark grounded in real e-commerce workflows, where each instance provides a reference rendering and an exported intermediate representation that may contain extraction errors. 1D is short for one day, representing the efficient completion of design-to-code tasks in less than one day. Models take both as input, using the intermediate representation as structural cues while being evaluated against the reference rendering, which tests robustness to intermediate representation defects rather than literal adherence. 1D-Bench requires generating an executable React codebase under a fixed toolchain with an explicit component hierarchy, and defines a multi-round setting in which models iteratively apply component-level edits using execution feedback. Experiments on commercial and open-weight multimodal models show that iterative editing generally improves final performance by increasing rendering success and often improving visual similarity. We further conduct a pilot study on post-training with synthetic repair trajectories and reinforcement learning based editing, and observe limited and unstable gains that may stem from sparse terminal rewards and high-variance file-level updates. The data and scripts used in this study are available in an anonymized repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/d2c-benchmark-A9C4/.

title: From Typist to Collaborator: A Systematic Review of AI’s Impact on Programming Efficiency and the Shift in Developer Roles
abstract: With continuous advancements in AI and large language models, AI in programming has evolved from simple code completion to intelligent agents with contextual understanding. This change has not only had a significant impact on the field of programming but also on programmers' employment. This paper aims to explore new working models for future programmers and analyze the efficiency and potential risks of AI programming. This paper systematically reviews key empirical studies from relevant papers published between 2020 and 2025 and finds that AI exhibits significant efficiency issues in programming. On the one hand, in LeetCode, AI performs well on low-to-medium difficulty problems, and AI programming has already surpassed 85% of human programmers in algorithm competitions. On the other hand, the actual development efficiency of AI when handling large open-source projects actually decreases by approximately 19%, and a series of safety and efficiency issues are found in AI programming, such as code redundancy and over-coupling when writing large projects. This article explores the transformation of programmers from code writers to AI collaborators, examining the advantages and disadvantages of AI in programming. It also elaborates on the specific requirements for future programmers, such as a deeper understanding of the nature of tasks and the need to maintain a dynamic balance between programmers and AI to achieve greater efficiency in project completion.

title: A Review of Research on the Development of Artificial Intelligence Programming Agent-Assisted Software
abstract: The development of large language models has enabled AI-assisted programming to gradually expand from early code completion to requirements understanding, code generation, testing, debugging, and project maintenance. The programming intelligence agent formed on this basis is no longer just returning a piece of code based on user input, but can read project files, break down tasks, call terminals and testing tools, and repeatedly modify the program based on the running results. Based on 60 publicly searchable representative papers, this paper adopts a structured narrative review method to review the research progress from the aspects of code-based models, agent control mechanisms, repository-level systems, evaluation benchmarks, and human-computer collaboration evidence. It also compares the research scope and analysis focus with existing reviews on software engineering agents. This paper further utilizes method classification, performance statistics, and mechanism diagrams to analyze different technical approaches, focusing on issues such as reliability, contextual understanding in large-scale projects, security and privacy, evaluation and reproducibility, operating costs, and accountability and governance. Research shows that programming agents can reduce the cost of repetitive coding and help users lacking professional programming experience complete prototype development. However, its efficiency gains are significantly affected by task size, project familiarity, quality standards, and manual review costs, making it difficult to consistently understand requirements and guarantee overall quality in complex projects. Future research should shift from simply pursuing the quantity of code generated to building verifiable, explainable, traceable, and collaborative software development processes.

title: Autonomous Agents in Modern Software Engineering: From Copilots to System Architects
abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed modern software engineering, shifting the role of AI systems from code-generation assistants and copilots toward autonomous agents capable of planning, executing, evaluating, and coordinating complex software development tasks. This paper, “Autonomous Agents in Modern Software Engineering: From Copilots to System Architects,” explores this paradigm shift and examines how autonomous agents are redefining software development workflows, architectural decision making, testing, debugging, deployment, and system maintenance. Unlike conventional AI copilots, which primarily assist developers through suggestions and interactive code generation, autonomous agents can pursue high-level objectives, decompose tasks into manageable steps, interact with development tools, collaborate with other agents, and iteratively refine their outputs based on feedback.

title: Yuma-Code: Automating LLM Agent Generation from Natural Language Specifications
abstract: Agentic systems are a new generation of software engineering applications that go far beyond traditional systems. Automatic generation of such systems is a promising approach to accelerate development, disseminate engineering knowledge, and improve construction scalability. Despite advances in LLM-based code generation, existing approaches provide limited support for structured requirement elicitation, architecture-aware generation, and systematic behavioral evaluation of agent-based systems. We propose Yuma-Code, a CLI framework that transforms natural-language specifications into executable agent code through structured requirement elicitation, automatic architecture selection, and multi-agent orchestration with specialized roles for requirements engineering, architecture design, and test generation. We evaluate Yuma-Code against four state-of-the-art frameworks using Agent-GenBench, a benchmark encompassing four agent architectures (Simple, Tool, Memory, and MCP). Results show that Yuma-Code consistently achieves full specification compliance and generates evaluation artifacts via LLM-as-a-Judge across all scenarios. In more complex settings (MCP), it attains high clarity and relevance (0.97) and strong memory recall (0.85). Copilot CLI demonstrates competitive performance across configurations, while Gemini CLI achieves the strongest results in the Simple scenario. Spec-kit and Kiro frequently generated non-executable code. These results suggest that agent generation benefits from being treated as a structured software engineering process, and highlight behavioral validation as a critical yet underexplored dimension in current LLM-based code generation approaches.

title: Looks Right, Works Right: A Project-Level Benchmark for Multi-Screen Mobile App Generation
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models can convert visual designs directly into executable code, but real mobile products require multiple screenshots to become a buildable codebase with shared components and working navigation. This project-level setting exposes three limits of existing design-to-code benchmarks: they focus on single-page generation rather than complete codebases, cannot evaluate cross-page navigation, and do not measure project-wide maintainability. We introduce MobileForge, the first benchmark for project-level multi-screen mobile app generation, comprising 29 real mobile apps, 309 human-reviewed screens, structured page-relationship annotations, and 701 navigation test specifications. MobileForge supports five-axis evaluation of build, navigation, visual fidelity, code maintainability, and efficiency. We also propose state-isolated navigation testing to avoid cascading failures in navigation evaluation and an anchor-referenced list-wise visual evaluation protocol to improve visual-judge reliability. Across 174 end-to-end runs on six frontier multimodal LLMs, current models can build mobile-app projects that compile and reach the correct pages, but interactive navigation remains unreliable and visual fidelity and maintainability still lag. The benchmark and supporting materials are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MobileForge-E2E5/ .

title: Harness Engineering for AI Coding Agents: Emerging Practices and Principles
abstract: As LLM-based coding agents transition from research prototypes to production tools, practitioners are discovering that system reliability depends less on model capability than on the engineering of the surrounding environment. A nascent discipline, harness engineering, has emerged to address this gap, encompassing the design of constraints, feedback loops, context management strategies, and verification mechanisms that govern how coding agents operate within real codebases. However, current knowledge remains fragmented across blog posts, technical reports, and isolated case studies, with no unified framework to guide practitioners or researchers. In this paper, we synthesize early industry practices and formalize harness engineering for AI coding agents around three core dimensions: feedforward guides that steer agent behavior before execution, feedback sensors that enable self-correction, and context isolation mechanisms that maintain agent coherence over long-horizon tasks. We identify key open challenges, including behavioral verification, harness evaluability, and the co-evolution of models and harnesses. Our goal is to provide both a conceptual foundation and a practical reference for this rapidly forming field.

title: Scaling Human-AI Coding Collaboration Requires a Governable Consensus Layer
abstract: Vibe coding turns natural-language intent into working software, but code generation alone does not give humans and agents a shared account of what they are building. As collaboration spans participants, components, and releases, design choices must remain understandable and open to revision. We argue that scaling human and AI coding collaboration requires a governable consensus layer. Agentic Consensus organizes collaboration around a versioned project-state model linking selected intent, structural commitments, executable artifacts, and evidence. Participants can clarify intent before implementation and coordinate proposed changes against commitments that humans can inspect and revise. Bidirectional synchronization connects intended changes to implementation and exposes conflicts or stale evidence as artifacts evolve. We implemented its review workflow in Consensus Control. In a small exploratory human study, 10 participants used the system on projects from their everyday work and reported clearer, faster understanding of agent-submitted changes. A three-condition comparison with the same participants collected 60 responses, with near-ceiling decision scores and measured representation and pipeline costs. Our research agenda asks how shared project state can preserve human understanding and control as agent contributions accumulate.

title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution
abstract: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.

title: REAgent: Requirement-Driven LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution
abstract: Issue resolution aims to automatically generate patches from given issue descriptions and has attracted significant attention with the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs). However, due to the complexity of software issues and codebases, LLM-generated patches often fail to resolve corresponding issues. Although various advanced techniques have been proposed with carefully designed tools and workflows, they typically treat issue descriptions as direct inputs and largely overlook their quality (e.g., missing critical context or containing ambiguous information), which hinders LLMs from accurate understanding and resolution. To address this limitation, we draw on principles from software requirements engineering and propose REAgent, a requirement-driven LLM agent framework that introduces issue-oriented requirements as structured task specifications to better guide patch generation. Specifically, REAgent automatically constructs structured and information-rich issue-oriented requirements, identifies low-quality requirements, and iteratively refines them to improve patch correctness. We conduct comprehensive experiments on three widely used benchmarks using two advanced LLMs, comparing against five representative or state-of-the-art baselines. The results demonstrate that REAgent consistently outperforms all baselines, achieving an average improvement of 17.40% in terms of the number of successfully-resolved issues (% Resolved).

title: SkillForge: Self-Distilling Agents for Project-Specific Issue Resolution
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based agents have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in automated software issue resolution, yet they often struggle to resolve issues in a specific repository because they lack project-specific knowledge. Existing self-evolving approaches acquire such knowledge from repository history or online repair trajectories, but they either depend on available historical issue-resolution signals or incur substantial per-issue test-time exploration cost. In this paper, we propose SkillForge, a self-distillation framework that proactively acquires project-specific knowledge from the repository itself. Instead of waiting for real issues to expose project-specific knowledge gaps, SkillForge synthesizes project-specific issues by re-implementing test-covered core functionalities of the repository. By resolving these synthetic issues, SkillForge distills reusable project-specific knowledge into entity-grounded skills and associates them with relevant repository entities for future issue resolution. Extensive experiments using both open-source and closed-source models show that SkillForge consistently improves issue resolution performance over strong baselines. These results demonstrate that proactively acquiring project-specific knowledge before solving real issues substantially improves downstream software issue resolution.

title: Repo-To-Skill: Distilling GitHub Repositories Into AI4AI Skills
abstract: Autonomous agents are beginning to carry out machine-learning (ML) research end to end. These agents combine a model backbone with a harness for planning, execution, memory, and verification, but this architecture still leaves domain-specific know-how outside the agent. We call this missing layer operational knowledge, the know-how that separates knowing a method from making it work. That knowledge is not absent from the field. It appears in repositories and papers, but in forms written for human readers and too large to load during a task. Once distilled into compact, verified skills, this knowledge can be reused across tasks rather than rediscovered during each run. We present DisCo, a skill-powered research agent that creates skills and uses them during research. Its distillation runs in two complementary forms: task-agnostic, condensing the field's widely used repositories into reusable skills, and task-oriented, producing the skills a concrete task calls for. The former, applied across the open ecosystem, yields the AREX-Skill Library, with 5,000+ verified skills distilled from 1,000 widely used ML repositories and organized into 20 areas and 178 capability families. With the GPT-5.5 backbone, research harness, and downstream execution budget held fixed, the skill-equipped research agent scores 134.3% higher on MLE-bench, 34.4% higher on PaperBench, 9.2% higher on FrontierCS, and 14.0% higher on PassNet than the same agent without skills. These gains come from adding distilled operating context under that fixed setup.

title: AUTOMATION OF SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT PROCESSES USING LLM AGENTS: INDUSTRIAL DEPLOYMENT EXPERIENCE
abstract: The paper presents an industrial deployment experience of an LLM-agent-based automation loop for software development lifecycle processes — agents integrated into individual stages of the traditional lifecycle. The loop comprises planning with version-controlled plan documents, task decomposition, two-tier code review with independent verification of findings, codebase audits cross-checked by models from different vendors, and a CLI tool layer serving as a shared interface for humans and agents. The measurement methodology and quantitative results are reported: a twofold velocity increase under an unchanged estimation methodology, growth of tasks handled in parallel per engineer, and audit cycle indicators. The applicability limits of the approach and the human-orchestrator role are outlined.

title: Stdlib or Third-Party? Empirical Performance and Correctness of LLM-Assisted Zero-Dependency Python Libraries
abstract: Third-party Python libraries introduce dependency-management overhead, supply-chain risk, and deployment friction. We study when eliminating a dependency preserves enough correctness and performance to justify the gains in footprint, deployability, and trust surface. Our testbed is zerodep, 44 single-file, stdlib-only Python modules spanning 12 categories, each benchmarked against its reference library. Three performance regimes emerge. Stdlib-only implementations achieve parity (within 2x) in the majority of cases; many outperform their references by 5x-115x where architectural overhead dominates; and a clear cliff appears for C-extension-backed computation (image processing, binary serialization, low-level crypto), confirmed by PyPy JIT and profiling experiments. Beyond speed, stdlib modules reduce installed footprint by orders of magnitude (median 31 KB vs. 700 KB), import 2.2x faster, and eliminate 88 transitive dependencies maintained by 128 distinct PyPI accounts. Analysis of the LLM-assisted development process across all 44 modules shows that specification completeness, not model capability, is a strong predictor of generation success, and that contract-linked review reduces review volume by 5x while eliminating compatibility regressions. Together, these results turn dependency elimination from an anecdotal coding style into an evidence-based engineering tradeoff.

title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

title: Foundation AI Models and Autonomous Software Agents for Next-Generation Intelligent Computing Systems
abstract: Two once-separate research programs have converged over the past five years: large-scale foundation models trained on broad data and adaptable to many downstream tasks, and autonomous software agents capable of planning, invoking tools, and acting over extended horizons with limited human supervision. This convergence is reshaping the design of intelligent computing systems, which must now provision, orchestrate, and govern models that reason, plan, and act rather than simply classify or generate. This paper surveys the state of the art across three interlocking fields — foundation models, autonomous AI agents, and intelligent computing infrastructure — and proposes a unified four-layer conceptual architecture connecting them. We examine autonomous software engineering as a detailed case study, since it is the domain in which agentic foundation models have been most rigorously benchmarked, and we synthesize current evidence on capability, reliability, and residual failure modes. We then discuss cross-cutting challenges in trust, safety, evaluation methodology, and edge-cloud resource efficiency, and close with a set of open research directions. Rather than presenting new experimental results, this paper's contribution is an integrative synthesis and a conceptual framework intended to orient researchers and system designers working at the intersection of these fields.

title: Contract Before Code: Failure-Compiled Contracts for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can make many edits before testing a task-wide assumption about an API, authentication mode, environment, or persistent state. A late verifier then exposes that the implementation rests on a false premise. We call the missing step contract acquisition and propose Contract Before Code (CBC), harness-level middleware that compiles historical failures into executable preflight gates. CBC normalizes trajectories, extracts recurring failure signatures, and compiles contracts containing an applicability condition, a probe template, and a planning consequence. At inference time, it retrieves applicable contracts and runs instantiated probes before broad implementation work.
